articles.headline: Iran collects 38 medals in 2 days of 2026 Asian Para Games
articles.summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iranian athletes have claimed 38 medals, including 10 golds, during the first two days of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
articles.body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iranian athletes have claimed 38 medals, including 10 golds, during the first two days of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

Iran's haul comprises 10 gold, 12 silver and 16 bronze medals across several disciplines, including shooting, cycling, table tennis, judo and powerlifting, a report by Press TV said on Tuesday.

Para athletics has supplied the largest share of Iran's gold medals so far. Yasin Khosravi took the men's shot put title in the F56/F57 classification, while Mohammad Saber claimed gold in the F33 event. Saman Pakbaz and Amirhossein Alipour also topped their respective men's shot put competitions in the F12 and F11 classifications.

Iran added two more athletics golds in the women's javelin throw and men's javelin throw. Elham Salehi won the women's F52/F53/F54 event, while Erfan Bondori claimed the men's F53/F54 title.

The country's para taekwondo athletes also made a strong start. Amirmohammad Haghighatshenas captured gold in the men's K44 under-70-kilogram category, and Ailar Jami claimed the women's K44 under-47-kilogram title.

In para swimming, Sina Zeyghaminejad secured gold in the men's 100-meter freestyle S10 event. He also earned bronze in the men's 200-meter individual medley SM10, giving him two medals in the pool.

Faezeh Ahmadi added another gold for Iran in the women's P2 10-meter air pistol SH1 event in para shooting.

Iran's silver-medal tally has also grown across several sports. In para athletics, A. A. Mohammadi took silver in the women's shot put F33, while Mahdi Olad finished second in the men's shot put F11. Abolfazl Zarif earned silver in the men's 50-meter freestyle S9, and Shaahin Izadyar claimed silver in the men's 100-meter freestyle S10.

Other silver medals came from S. Javanmardi in para shooting, B. Farzad in para cycling, Z. Rahimi in para taekwondo, M. Tourani and Z. Moradi in women's javelin events, H. Safarzadeh in the women's 200-meter T12, A. Olfatnia in the men's long jump T37/T38, and P. Habibi in the women's club throw F32/F51.

Iran's bronze medals have come from a similarly broad range of disciplines. Para swimming contributed medals through A. Motallebi Fesharaki and A. Karimi Jahan, while M. Dalir secured bronze in the men's B 1,000-meter time trial in para cycling.

Iran also earned bronze medals in para athletics through A. Hemami, F. Sohrabitabar, H. Motaghian and R. Hatamishooli. Other bronze winners were H. Janfeshan in para table tennis, M. Borchlou and M. Gholamishafia in para judo, and M. Hassanpour, M. Abdollahpour Deroei, S. Sadeghianpour and P. M. Tourani in para taekwondo.

M. Bakhtiar added a bronze in men's para powerlifting in the up-to-72-kilogram category.

The fifth Asian Para Games, running from Oct. 18-24, bring together athletes from across Asia in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Iran entered the competition aiming to defend its second-place finish from the previous edition, held in Hangzhou in 2023 after a one-year postponement. The Iranian delegation comprises 166 athletes competing in 15 sports.

With several days of competition remaining, Iran will look to build on its early medal haul as athletes continue to compete across the Games' program.

Haghighatshenas faced Japan’s Shunsuke Kudo in the men’s K44 under-70kg final at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 on Tuesday. The Iranian athlete won both rounds, with scores of 14–2 and 18–12, to secure the gold medal, Tehran Times reported.

On his way to the final, Haghighatshenas defeated Kazakhstan’s Din Muhammad Askar in the quarterfinals and overcame his Uzbek opponent in the semifinals before beating Kudo in the final.

With this victory, Iran’s para taekwondo team concluded the second day of competition with five medals: Haghighatshenas won gold, Zahra Rahimi claimed silver, and Parimah Tourani, Saeed Sadeghianpour, and Maryam Abdollahpour each earned a bronze medal.

articles.headline: Cui Zhe wins China's first gold, Guo Lingling sets world record at Asian Para Games
articles.summary: Cui Zhe claimed China's first gold medal and Guo Lingling set a world record in para powerlifting on the opening day of the 5th Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
articles.body_text:
(ECNS) -- Cui Zhe claimed China's first gold medal and Guo Lingling set a world record in para powerlifting on the opening day of the 5th Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

Cui won the women's 41kg title with three successful lifts, including a third-attempt 120kg that surpassed her personal best of 119kg set at the Paris Paralympics. The victory extended her gold-medal streak to five consecutive Asian Para Games.

Guo won the women's 45kg event with a world-record lift of 126kg. She said she is confident of competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics if her health and form allow. Chen Liuxun took bronze in the men's 49kg category, China's first medal of the Games.

China's swimmers collected 14 gold, 12 silver and 6 bronze medals, breaking multiple Games records and sweeping the podium in several events. In wheelchair fencing, China won all four golds on offer, with Zhong Saichun and Qin Benjun winning the men's foil individual A and B titles, and Gu Haiyan and Kang Su taking the two women's titles. Li Huiling and Wang Xiaomei won the women's C4-5 1,000m time trial and C1-3 3,000m individual pursuit in track cycling, respectively.

In athletics, He Shanshan won the women's 1,500m T11 title in a Games-record 4:41.19, and Mi Na took gold in the women's discus throw F37/F38. China's women's wheelchair basketball team beat Laos 109-20, the women's sitting volleyball team defeated Iran 3-0, and the goalball teams beat Japan 1-0 in the women's event and South Korea 9-4 in the men's event.

articles.headline: China sends biggest-ever delegation abroad to Asian Para Games in Japan
articles.summary: The 5th Asian Para Games opened in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Sunday, with China sending 312 athletes to compete across 17 sports and 335 events — its largest-ever delegation for an overseas edition of the Games.
articles.body_text:
(ECNS) -- The 5th Asian Para Games opened in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Sunday, with China sending 312 athletes to compete across 17 sports and 335 events — its largest-ever delegation for an overseas edition of the Games.

The Games, running from Oct. 18 to 24 under the theme "Imagine One Heart," bring together nearly 3,000 para athletes from 45 countries and regions across Asia, competing in about 500 events across 18 sports.

Chinese para taekwondo athlete Li Yujie and para powerlifter Yan Panpan served as flagbearers for the Chinese delegation during the opening ceremony at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium.

The Chinese delegation totals around 500 members, including 312 athletes with an average age of about 28.8. All Chinese athletes are amateurs from diverse backgrounds, including workers, students, office employees and freelancers.

This marks China's fifth participation in the Asian Para Games.

The Asian Para Games are organized by the Asian Paralympic Committee, a regional organization of the International Paralympic Committee, and succeeded the Far East and South Pacific Games for the Disabled, which began in 1975. Since the 2010 Guangzhou Asian Games, the Asian Para Games have been held in the same city and the same year as the Asian Games.

articles.body_text:
CAIRO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian discussed mediation efforts and regional developments during a meeting with Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir in Tehran, Iran's Nournews reported on Tuesday.

Pakistan is a key mediator between the US and Iran. Its earlier mediation efforts with both parties resulted in an interim peace agreement ​signed in ⁠June. But the Islamabad Memorandum quickly faltered, amid new fighting between Iran and the US weeks after.

Munir also met Iranian parliament speaker Mohammed Baqer Qalibaf. The Iranian official said Washington can't earn Tehran's trust until it fulfills the seven conditions presented by Iran for reopening of the Strait of Hormuz last month, according to an Iranian readout of the meeting.

Iran's conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, ‌the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts.

(Reporting by Menna Alaa El-Din and Yasmine Ghania, Editing by Alexandra Hudson)

articles.headline: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
articles.summary: Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Carney's push for national unity.(Image credit: Ty O'Neil)
articles.body_text:
A voting location in Wainwright, Alberta, is seen on Monday. Ty O'Neil/AP hide caption

EDMONTON, Alberta — Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for national unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and annexation threats.

With more than 1.5 million votes counted, 76% supported remaining in Canada, while close to 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.

The referendum wasn't a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney signs an autograph as he attends a national unity rally in Red Deer, Alberta, Oct. 16. John Ulan/The Canadian Press via AP hide caption

"Albertans made a clear choice," Carney said. "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada."

Carney said that the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its center.

Alberta's separatists, however, saw a silver lining.

"We don't have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better," said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada.

"Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada," Smith posted on social media.

Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta's future.

"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.

Political signs are posted on a property's fence in Wainwright, Alberta, Canada, Monday. Ty O'Neil/AP hide caption

Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday.

Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.

Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that won't disappear.

Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity.

"Vote like Canada's future depends on it, because it does," he told a rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.

Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said.

Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.

At a separatist referendum night gathering at an Edmonton restaurant, the crowd fell quiet as results rolled in.

"We're not going anywhere," said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project. "We've dominated the conversation in the last year. We've been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we're going to continue moving forward."

Rath had said he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as leader of her governing United Conservative Party and said the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party.

Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Canada's federal government.

"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything."

Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than healthcare.

With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, "It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we're fighting among ourselves."

articles.headline: Alberta voters decide whether to take a step toward separating from Canada
articles.summary: In Canada, the oil-rich province of Alberta votes in a referendum that could set it on a path toward separation, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warns of threats to Canadian unity.
articles.body_text:
In Canada, the oil-rich province of Alberta votes in a referendum that could set it on a path toward separation, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warns of threats to Canadian unity.

Voters in Alberta, Canada, are deciding today whether to take the first step toward a referendum on separating from the rest of the country. Reporter Sheena Rossiter joins us from Edmonton, which is the capital of Alberta. Hi there.

SHEENA ROSSITER, BYLINE: Hello.

SUMMERS: So, Sheena, this vote's a nonbinding referendum. Explain for us a bit more what people in Alberta are voting on today.

ROSSITER: Well, essentially, it's a vote on whether to have another referendum. There are 10 questions covering everything from immigration and provincial services to Alberta's constitutional status. Question 10 is the key one. Voters choose between keeping Alberta in Canada or starting the process towards a separation referendum. If Option 2 wins, it could pave the way for a vote on separation, much like Brexit in the U.K.

SUMMERS: And these separatist sentiments there, how long have they been brewing in Alberta?

ROSSITER: These grievances go back decades. Some people I spoke with at the Alberta independence rally have been separatists for 25 years, like Cory Morgan. He is the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group advocating for an independent Alberta.

CORY MORGAN: Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand something large is brewing here. And if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow.

ROSSITER: Separatist sentiment really grew during COVID, with frustration spilling onto the streets during the 2022 trucker convoy in Ottawa. Now, the premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, called for a referendum but wants Alberta to stay in Canada. And Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, is making the same case, saying, quote, "Canada is stronger together."

SUMMERS: What's really at the heart of this, though?

ROSSITER: Well, Alberta is a major oil-producing province. It's the wealthiest province in the Canadian Confederation, and some residents feel that they contribute more to Canada than they get back. They want to keep more of that money in Alberta. But a government-commissioned report from the University of Calgary estimates that Alberta separating from Canada could cost up to $170 billion Canadian over five years. Thomas Lukaszuk, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity group campaigning against Alberta separation, points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic fallout.

THOMAS LUKASZUK: Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces. And till today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that.

SUMMERS: How soon will we know the results?

ROSSITER: Well, Elections Alberta says unofficial results are expected within 48 hours of polls closing. There's also a legal challenge over Indigenous rights, with the province appealing a court ruling that First Nations weren't properly consulted. And whatever the result, Alberta's place in Canada is likely to remain a major issue heading into next year's provincial election.

SUMMERS: Sheena Rossiter, reporting from Edmonton, Alberta, thanks much.

articles.body_text:
Iran's ambassador to Baghdad on Tuesday said Iraq has agreed to either expel Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in the Kurdistan region or hand them over to Tehran.

The claim by Mohammad Al Sadegh came after he had attended a meeting of the Iraq-Iran joint security committee in Baghdad on Monday. Qasim Al Aboudi, the National Security Adviser, led the Iraqi delegation, which also featured representatives of the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region.

In a statement on X, Mr Al Sadegh said both sides had agreed “to remove elements of Iranian separatist terrorist groups from the Kurdistan region of Iraq or hand them over to Iran”.

There was no immediate comment from the Iraqi government or the Kurdistan region, nor from Mr Al Aboudi.

An official Iraqi readout of the meeting said both sides had discussed implementing the joint security agreement and the “outstanding files and problems”, and identified the “appropriate solutions”.

The apparent deal came only days after Iraq's parliament endorsed Yassir Al Maliki, the son-in-law of the pro-Iran State of Law Coalition leader and former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki, as Interior Minister.

Iraq and Iran signed a bilateral security agreement in March 2023, under which Baghdad committed to disarming Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and relocating them from the border area, and preventing Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on Iran.

'My soul is Iraqi, my heart is Emirati': Iraqi community comes together in celebration in Dubai

Groups such as the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran, Komala, the Free Life Party of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Freedom Party were to hand over their heavy weapons and move to camps farther from the border. Iraqi officials said at the time families would be relocated to five designated camps in the Kurdistan region while the UN refugee agency would process asylum claims.

The groups, some of which have been based in northern Iraq since the 1980s – after the Islamic Revolution and during the Iran-Iraq war – are seeking greater rights for Iran's Kurdish minority. Tehran accuses them of terrorism and of fuelling unrest, such as the 2022 protests that followed the death of Mahsa Amini.

In a sign of growing pressure on Baghdad and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region, over the presence of these groups, Nechirvan Barzani, President of Kurdistan Region, said last week: “Unfortunately, the [Iranian] Kurdish opposition forces acted in a highly irresponsible manner and placed the Kurdistan region in an extremely difficult position.

“An armed force cannot view the Kurdistan region as a safe haven and then operate from its territory to threaten a neighbouring country,” he said, in reference to reports that the groups were planning to move into Iran, with US backing.

Implementation of the security agreement has been uneven. Baghdad says it has moved fighters from border areas and closed some headquarters, while Tehran has repeatedly called the measures insufficient and continued to carry out drone and missile strikes on opposition camps in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah provinces.

Expelling these groups or handing them over to Iran would mark a significant hardening of Iraq's position if confirmed, raising legal and humanitarian questions given that thousands of Iranian Kurdish refugees live in Iraq, most in the Kurdistan region.

The Kurdistan Regional Government has previously opposed forced return, calling for a peaceful resolution that respects Iraq's constitution, which bars armed groups from threatening neighbours, while also protecting refugee rights.

articles.body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) –Iran's First Vice President Mohammadreza Aref has said Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) must move beyond merely condemning US-Israeli aggression and sanctions imposed against Iran, and also strengthen its economic power.

Speaking at the meeting of Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO)’s Prime Ministers, held in Tajik capital of Dushanbe, the vice president emphasized the economic consequences of the US unilateral measures taken against the independent states.

In the beginning, Aref thanked the government and people of Tajikistan for hosting the meeting and praised the SCO secretary-general and his colleagues for facilitating the gathering.

A sustainable response to shared economic threats cannot be limited merely to condemning them; rather, Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) members must strengthen their own economic capacities., he opined.

Aref presented Iran’s proposals for accelerating the establishment of an independent development bank, forming an energy consortium, expanding trade using national currencies, and developing transit corridors.

He cited the deaths of more than 157 schoolchildren children in Minab Elementary School during the US-Israeli military aggression waged against Iran on February 28, stating that education is a fundamental human right.

Aref said the United States and Israel violated the international law, the UN Charter and international humanitarian law during their February 28 military aggression waged against Iran.

The vice president went on to say that attacks killed the Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei and schoolchildren on the first day, as well as numerous other innocent civilians, and targeted residential, educational, and medical facilities and infrastructure.

He added that Iran’s Armed Forces and united people inflicted a heavy defeat on the aggressors.

The Iranian vice president also expressed appreciation for the SCO and its member states for condemning the aggressors and armed attacks, highlighting the need to hold those responsible accountable.

He said it was encouraging to see cultural and humanitarian engagement within the organization, underscoring the importance of strengthening cooperation on humanitarian issues.

The remarks come amid heightened US military activity in West Asia and increasingly hostile rhetoric by American officials against the Islamic Republic.

Tehran has repeatedly warned that US bases and naval assets across the region will be targeted in response to any renewed aggression against Iranian territory.

articles.summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said trade between Iran and Tajikistan has grown 50% in recent months despite the imposed war on Iran.
articles.body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said trade between Iran and Tajikistan has grown 50% in recent months despite the imposed war on Iran.

Aref made the remarks in a meeting with Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, where he thanked the Tajik government and people for their sympathetic positions toward Iran during the Ramadan war and stressed the need to draw on historical, cultural and linguistic commonalities to advance relations. Aref pointed to the deep civilizational ties between the two countries and said a joint high committee on Persian and ancestral language, literature, culture and civilization could help preserve the shared heritage. Aref said that despite the growth, cooperation capacity far exceeds current levels and that existing opportunities should be used to develop economic and trade ties. He also stressed expanding scientific, technological, cultural and tourism cooperation. Aref voiced Iran's readiness to cooperate with Tajikistan in oil and gas exploration, petrochemical industries and exports of oil and gas products, and welcomed Rahmon's proposal for a South Pars-Afghanistan-Tajikistan energy corridor, describing it as a positive and constructive plan presented to Iran's president. He said Iran is interested in expanding trilateral cooperation with Tajikistan and Afghanistan and that suitable capacities exist. The meeting also stressed exports of Iranian oil products to Tajikistan and Iranian help in connecting the country to the open waters of the Persian Gulf. On the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, Aref said it has an important capacity to link regional security and stability with economic development and greater connectivity among member states, and that this should be used to expand cooperation in trade, transit, energy and infrastructure connectivity. He said Iran and Tajikistan can cooperate more closely within the SCO on transit corridors, border security, counterterrorism, counter-narcotics and Afghanistan developments, and stressed greater coordination on shared regional issues. Aref pointed to the two countries' scientific and technological capacities and said implementing an agreement to launch a joint Iran-Tajikistan technology center could pave the way for joint activities and expanded scientific and technological cooperation. Both sides stressed operationalizing the center. On international cooperation, Aref said the two countries have had good cooperation in international bodies and have supported each other's positions, and that this coordination should be strengthened at regional and international levels. The two sides also stressed preserving Iranian culture and civilization and the shared heritage of Persian speakers, expanding tourism and cultural cooperation, and strengthening scientific and economic ties. articles.summary: Sarah Helm, the writer and wife of Britain’s National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, has called for the UK's ban on the Palestine Action group to be lifted, after a police investigation into her social media posts.The UK has proscribed the pro-Palestine group as a terrorist organisation and expressing support for the group is a criminal offence.Police said at the weekend they closed their investigation of an earlier post by Ms Helm, and decided they would take no action as it did not meet the criminal threshold.On Monday, Ms Helm asked: “Where do I sign?” in response to a letter calling for the ban to be lifted and backing Irish author Sally Rooney and her publisher Faber after they decided her books would no longer be sold in the UK.Ms Rooney had been warned her plan to donate earnings from sales could be considered a criminal offence.Ms Helm, a former Middle East correspondent for The Independent newspaper, had written “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” in response to a clip criticising Ms Rooney.Her stance on Palestine Action, which was banned in the UK in 2025 after an attack on a UK airbase, has led to questions whether it will affect Mr Powell’s role within government. More than 3,500 people have been arrested for supporting Palestine Action in the UK, mostly for holding up placards at demonstrations.Last month, the UK imposed sanctions aimed at illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the Israeli government was turning a blind eye to the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians.Mr Powell visited Israel earlier this month in a bid to persuade the Israeli government not to close the UK’s Consulate General in Jerusalem, in response to the sanctions. The Consulate opened in 1838 and handles the country's relations with Palestinians in ​the city as ⁠well as in the West Bank and Gaza. Rwandan Govt Critic Found Beheaded in Uganda

Robert Kabera, a 50-year-old former Rwandan army sergeant major and outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded on the outskirts of Kampala, Uganda. Kabera had fled Rwanda and sought asylum in Uganda, citing political persecution. He later gained a following through his YouTube channel, which featured criticism of Kagame's government. Ugandan police said his head had not been recovered. His widow expressed fears for her family's safety. The opposition Rwanda National Congress has called for a thorough investigation, as his killing renews concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile. Other critics of Kagame have been killed abroad, including former intelligence chief Patrick Karegeya, who was found dead in Johannesburg in 2014.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

UN Condemns Deadly Drone Strikes Across Sudan

Drone strikes across Sudan have killed and injured civilians, including children, as fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces continues to intensify. The attacks injured at least 19 people at a market in Abyei and targeted locations in Khartoum, including an area near the airport. The strikes reportedly killed at least 19 people, including 10 children, across several states. The United Nations condemned the attacks and raised concerns over the targeting of humanitarian workers, with 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers reportedly killed since the conflict began in April 2023. An estimated 20 million people face acute hunger, with famine risks rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Despite the insecurity, aid agencies continue delivering assistance, including restoring water supplies to thousands of people in Central Darfur. Sudan's humanitarian response plan remains just over 43% funded.

Zimbabwe's Ruling Party to Discipline MPs Who Missed Constitutional Amendment Vote

Zimbabwe's ruling Zanu-PF party plans to discipline Members of Parliament who failed to attend crucial parliamentary sittings during consideration of Constitutional Amendment No. 3 Bill. Party legal secretary Ziyambi Ziyambi announced the sanctions at the party's annual conference in Chinhoyi, naming several senior officials and deputy ministers among those who did not vote, although their reasons remain unclear. The disciplinary move comes as Zanu-PF advances resolutions to postpone its next elective congress from 2027 to 2029, potentially keeping President Emmerson Mnangagwa at the helm until 2030. Provincial leaders defended resolutions supporting his continued leadership and called for constitutional alignment and greater national self-sufficiency in areas such as medicine, technology and industrial production.

Thabo Mbeki Denies Blocking Apartheid-Era Prosecutions at Inquiry Commission

Former South African president Thabo Mbeki has denied allegations that he held secret meetings with former apartheid-era military and police generals to prevent prosecutions for human rights abuses. Testifying before the Khampepe Commission of Inquiry into delayed Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) prosecutions, Mbeki said the generals approached him in 1996 seeking a meeting with the ANC over amnesty applications. He argued that former president FW de Klerk and his cabinet should also apply. Mbeki said the ANC subsequently pursued collective amnesty for some of its leaders to encourage the apartheid leadership to do the same, but the courts later overturned the decision. He maintained that his administration never directed the National Prosecuting Authority to halt or suppress investigations, arguing that prosecutions were the NPA's responsibility. He also defended his 2003 parliamentary speech and later arrangements involving pardon requests, saying these aimed to encourage truth-telling rather than grant blanket immunity to those responsible for apartheid-era crimes.

articles.body_text:
Kenya Confirms Eighth Ebola Case

Kenya's Health Ministry has confirmed another Ebola infection, bringing the country's total to eight as the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) continues to spread. Health Ministry Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said the latest patient is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker and developed fever, headaches and muscle pain. He worked as a patient attendant, cleaning utensils and linen. He was likely exposed to Kenya's first Ebola patient, who died on October 5. Amoth said authorities tested 38 people, with one testing positive, while six other patients in quarantine remained stable after receiving supportive treatment. Meanwhile, authorities in the DR Congo reported that the outbreak had reached an eighth province, Nord-Ubangi, where two cases, including one death, were recorded near the border with the Central African Republic. The DR Congo has reported at least 9,400 cases and more than 4,500 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

Kenyan Court to Deliver Verdict in Paul Mackenzie Mass Murder Case

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

A Kenyan court is set to deliver its judgment in the mass murder case against doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie and 29 of his followers, who are accused of murdering 191 children in the Shakahola forest. Prosecutors allege that the children were forced to starve to death as part of a religious doctrine that promised they would meet Jesus, while education and modern medicine were portrayed as evil. Mackenzie and the co-accused have pleaded not guilty, maintaining that nobody was forced to die. The case marks the first time Mackenzie will face a verdict on the most serious murder charges, although he and other leaders face additional cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and the denial of education to children. Authorities discovered more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the coastal forest, where Mackenzie had encouraged followers from across Kenya to settle and observe his teachings. Survivors and witnesses have described widespread starvation, the rejection of medical treatment and the deaths of children and adults. One survivor, Peter Shukrani, said he nearly died after his mother discarded his medication because she believed medicine was forbidden by the preacher's doctrine. Stephen Mwiti, meanwhile, said he lost all six of his children in the forest. Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, initially accused in the case, entered a plea deal and became a prosecution witness.

Drone Strikes Kill Civilians in Sudan as Fire Destroys Market Stalls

Drone attacks killed civilians, including women, in Sudan's West Darfur and West Kordofan regions on Saturday, as separate strikes targeted military installations in the east and a fire destroyed dozens of commercial stalls in Northern State. In West Darfur, a drone attack attributed to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) killed several people, including six women, and injured five others in Bir Saliba, Sarba locality. Most of the victims were reportedly displaced people who had travelled to the area for agricultural work. In West Kordofan, the Kordofan Observatory said a drone strike carried out by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) hit a civilian lorry near Ankush, killing four people, including three women, and injuring others. The passengers included patients travelling for medical treatment and civilians heading to shop. The Observatory also reported other recent drone attacks that killed civilians, including a child, and warned that targeting civilians and civilian vehicles could violate international humanitarian law and amount to war crimes. It called on the SAF to halt attacks on civilians and urged the RSF to keep away from residential areas. Meanwhile, drone attacks targeted military installations in El Gedaref, Khashm El Girba and the Upper Atbara and Setit Dam Complex on Sunday, with air defences reportedly intercepting several drones. No casualties were reported from those strikes. In Northern State, a fire destroyed between 75 and 80 stalls at El Burgeig market on Saturday evening. Initial reports suggested an electrical fault triggered the blaze, which spread rapidly through stalls containing goods, including perfume.

Ebola Vaccine Trials Offer Hope

Vaccine candidates undergoing clinical trials offer hope of protection against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola responsible for the Democratic Republic of the Congo's worst-ever outbreak, according to Emanuele Capobianco, director of global health security at Gavi, the global vaccine alliance. The outbreak has surpassed 9,000 reported cases, with more than 4,000 deaths, but no vaccine or specific treatment has been approved for this strain. A clinical trial of the existing Ervebo vaccine, which is approved for the more common Zaire strain, is expected to assess whether it provides cross-protection against Bundibugyo. Meanwhile, vaccines developed by the University of Oxford, in partnership with the Serum Institute of India, and US-based Moderna are undergoing early-stage trials. They are due to report from phase one trials later this October and, if the results are safe and show good immune responses, larger phase two and three trials may follow. If development progresses successfully, a rollout could begin in the first half of 2027. Gavi has committed US$50 million to support the outbreak response, including vaccine access, and 70,000 doses of Ervebo were released from the global stockpile in August at the request of the Congolese government. Capobianco stressed that the outbreak could still be contained through early detection, surveillance, infection prevention and timely treatment, even before new vaccines become available. He said many deaths occur in communities before patients reach health facilities, highlighting the need to improve access to care and build public trust through healthcare workers, local leaders and community engagement. Research could also help establish a future global stockpile for Bundibugyo, protecting against subsequent outbreaks.

Madagascar Marks One Year Since Uprising as Russian Influence Grows

Madagascar has marked one year since military leader Michael Randrianirina took power following youth-led protests that forced elected president Andry Rajoelina from office, but many of the reforms demanded by demonstrators remain unfinished as Russia expands its influence in the country. Randrianirina was sworn in as president on October 17, 2025, after protests over water and electricity shortages, justice and transparency. Russia quickly established ties with the new administration, and researchers say Moscow has since expanded its military, political and economic presence. An investigation by All Eyes on Wagner found that Russian military personnel linked to Africa Corps, the organisation that succeeded the Wagner Group, arrived in Madagascar to train the military, while shipments of helicopters, tanks, trucks, drones and rifles were delivered as donations. Russia has also reportedly expanded its influence through African Initiative, a news agency linked to the Russian state, which has engaged young people, supported local media and organised trips to Moscow for media figures and influencers. Researchers have highlighted Russia's interest in the northern port of Antsiranana, also known as Diego-Suarez, whose strategic position near the Mozambique Channel could offer access to major Indian Ocean shipping routes. Madagascar and Russia announced a joint economic zone in May, with fuel storage identified as an initial project. Analysts say the relationship could eventually support broader military, logistical and financial operations. However, political observers warn that the changes promised after the uprising have not translated into substantial institutional reform. Transparency International's vice-chair, Ketakandriana Rafitoson, said longstanding problems, including weak checks and balances, a lack of transparency and impunity, remain. Young activists who helped drive the protests have also expressed frustration over their limited influence in the transition, while victims of the previous regime's violence continue to await justice.

UK Threatens Visa Ban on Eritreans Over Deportation Dispute

UK Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has threatened to ban all Eritrean nationals from entering the UK unless the East African country agrees to accept more of its citizens facing deportation, including foreign national offenders. Initial measures, which took effect, restrict Eritrean diplomats from travelling more than 60km outside London without permission. The UK will also stop fast-track visas for VIPs. Eritrea has condemned the move as a political gimmick, accusing the UK of failing to engage in meaningful dialogue and disputing claims about cooperation on returns. The UK government maintains that Eritrea withdrew its cooperation earlier this year. However, migration experts have questioned whether the restrictions will be effective. They said that many Eritrean asylum seekers qualify for protection because of repression and forced military conscription in their home country.

DR Congo Ebola Outbreak Response Progresses in Bunia

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Efforts to contain the Democratic Republic of Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak are showing progress in Bunia, Ituri province, where health workers are intensifying community awareness campaigns and home visits to encourage residents to seek medical care. The outbreak has reportedly killed more than 4,000 people in five months. It was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization. Fear of infection and misinformation have disrupted healthcare services, particularly maternity care, with maternal deaths in Bunia rising from an average of three to almost five a week, according to health officials. UNICEF has established 12 nurseries linked to health facilities to care for children separated from parents receiving Ebola treatment. Survivors are helping support vulnerable children. Despite improvements in community trust and healthcare attendance, the outbreak continues in other areas, where armed-group activity and insufficient humanitarian funding are hampering response efforts.

China Outlines Four Principles to Resolve Conflicts Across Africa

Chinese President Xi Jinping has outlined four principles for resolving conflicts in Africa. He has called for African-led solutions, respect for national sovereignty, an end to hostilities and efforts to address the root causes of insecurity. Speaking during a meeting with Togo's President of the Council of Ministers, Faure Essozimna Gnassingbé, in Beijing on October 13, Xi said African people should remain central to decisions affecting the continent. He urged parties involved in conflict resolution to respect the United Nations Charter, pursue dialogue and compromise, and combine immediate security measures with long-term development planning. His remarks come as several African regions, including Sudan, the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa, continue to face conflict and security challenges. The two leaders also agreed to strengthen China-Togo relations through cooperation in trade, infrastructure, renewable energy, digital technology and industrialisation. Xi encouraged Togo to take advantage of China's zero-tariff arrangements for African products.

Kenya Reflects on Raila Odinga Legacy One Year After His Death

One year after former Kenyan Prime Minister Raila Odinga's death, his legacy continues to shape debates about democracy, constitutional reform and the future of opposition politics. Odinga spent decades campaigning for multiparty democracy and played a significant role in Kenya's political reforms, including the adoption of the 2010 Constitution. His supporters credit him with promoting reconciliation and institutional change. His political alliances with former foes, critics said, diluted the opposition's ability to hold the government to account. His Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) party's future has also been in the spotlight, with party leaders warning it is in danger of losing its identity and support among ordinary Kenyans. His daughter Winnie Odinga has declared interest in the Nairobi Senate seat in the upcoming 2027 polls. As younger generations reflect on his contribution, questions remain over whether Kenya's political institutions and opposition parties will uphold the democratic principles associated with his legacy.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel, as the two sides discuss the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran, American media reported.

The meeting, which was also attended by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, took place on Monday evening at Ovda Airbase in southern Israel, Axios said in a report quoting two sources. The visit was also reported by CNN, which quoted two sources and a US official. The Pentagon has declined to comment on Mr Hegseth’s movements.

He was also reported to have met US troops at the base and later posted an image of himself visiting personnel from US Central Command, which oversees American military operations across the Middle East.

Trump endorses Netanyahu for Israeli election

The visit came days before Israel’s October 27 election and a day after US President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Mr Netanyahu, calling him a “great warrior prime minister”.

In footage shared by Mr Netanyahu on Tuesday, the Israeli leader thanked Mr Trump for his support and described him as “by far, the greatest friend Israel has ever had and will have in the White House”.

“Donald, we have a job to finish. You said it, and we’ll finish it together,” Mr Netanyahu said.

Mr Netanyahu said the alliance between the two countries had demonstrated that they could achieve significant results together. He added there was scope to expand the Abraham Accords, which established relations between Israel and several Arab states during Mr Trump’s first term in office.

Mr Netanyahu also praised the US President for confronting what he described as the greatest danger facing Americans – an Iran armed with nuclear weapons. “We won’t let it happen,” he said.

Mr Trump’s endorsement appeared to reflect shared strategic interests over Iran, as well as the political importance of maintaining a close relationship with Mr Netanyahu during a volatile period for the region. The backing also gives Mr Netanyahu a boost before the election as he seeks to present his relationship with Washington as an asset for Israeli security. Mr Trump, meanwhile, has an interest in maintaining a reliable Israeli partner as his administration pursues its regional objectives.

But the two leaders have reportedly differed over the direction of the Iran war and the prospects for diplomatic initiatives in Gaza and elsewhere. There has been no public confirmation of a specific agreement linking the endorsement to Israeli policy concessions or renewed military action.

Hegseth said in a social media post that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.

Israel's Army Radio reported his meeting with Netanyahu took place at an air force base in Israel's southern desert.

Hegseth's visit comes amid rising tensions in the Middle East war as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

It also came a day after US President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel, the country's first ballot since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel.

US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war. Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he's not seeking to attack Iran before the October 27 Israeli election. Trump has said he will not attack Iran before US midterm elections in November.

articles.body_text:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu basked in Donald Trump's endorsement on Monday ahead of close-fought elections, airing a phone call in which the US president predicted he would win and suggested they may again attack Iran together.

A day after Trump publicly endorsed Netanyahu for the October 27 vote, Netanyahu put out a video of a telephone call in which the two right-wing leaders lavish praise on each other.

"I think you're going to have a tremendous victory, actually," Trump can be heard saying on speakerphone.

"You're the man I want by my side, Bibi," Trump said, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.

Netanyahu -- while reminding the famously loose-lipped president that they were on an open line -- hailed Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in February.

"Donald, we have a job to finish," Netanyahu beamed. "We'll finish it together. We'll finish it, and no one else will do it."

Netanyahu did not elaborate but again described Iran's clerical state, which remains in power nearly eight months after the joint attack, as "the greatest danger".

Netanyahu appeared to be speaking to Trump from an air force base from which he earlier released a video warning that he had been assured of Israel's "capability to strike our enemies the moment it is required".

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, had waited for years for a US president who would agree to attack Iran. But Trump abruptly switched course in April and reached a ceasefire with Tehran that is now in tatters.

Polls showed Trump's approval rating in Israel plunged afterwards.

An Axios report on Tuesday that US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met Netanyahu in Israel the previous day added to speculation that US-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.

The Pentagon declined to comment on the reported meeting.

David Makovsky, a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said it was unclear whether Trump's endorsement would have a "huge impact" on the Israeli electorate.

Netanyahu is "a polarising figure. You either love him or hate him," Makovsky said. "How many undecideds are there? Not that many."

Trump went ahead with the endorsement despite open tensions involving top US officials. Vice President JD Vance has issued stinging criticism of Israel over the Iran war, saying it had no friends other than the United States and needs to get in line with US policy.

Makovsky said Trump's move may indicate that he secured an agreement from Netanyahu in return for the endorsement, although it was unclear on what.

The Israel Hayom newspaper -- in a report denied by the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee -- said recently that the Trump administration was pushing Netanyahu to form a government that no longer includes his far-right allies, who have championed settler extremists in the West Bank and urged the expulsion of all of Gaza's Palestinians.

The newspaper said that a more moderate new unity government could then work on normalising Israel's relations with more Arab and Islamic states. Netanyahu mentioned in the call to Trump expanding the so-called Abraham Accords, in which the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco normalised with Israel in 2020.

Netanyahu described Trump as "by far, the greatest friend Israel has ever had".

Since his first term, Trump has taken several major steps to back Israel, including moving the US embassy to Jerusalem, which most countries do not recognise as Israel's capital due to the dispute with the Palestinians.

Netanyahu's top challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, voiced respect for Trump after the endorsement, but insisted, "Only Israelis can choose their leader."

Trump, 80, and Netanyahu, who turns 77 on Wednesday, have forged a close partnership at a time when both are vastly unpopular in public opinion in most democratic nations.

The pair have also managed to avoid prosecution while in power, with Netanyahu facing charges of corruption that could land him in prison.

Trump, who remains bitter over cases against him including over his attempts to overturn his 2020 election loss, told Netanyahu he was a "warrior" who had been "treated unfairly by your country and by some others."

Netanyahu faces an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the relentless Israeli offensive in Gaza in response to the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks.

Netanyahu has denounced the charges, while the Trump administration has tried to dismantle the court in The Hague through sanctions.

singles.summary: The prices of food and fuel have doubled in the city of Taiz as it struggles under a Houthi siege, the UN warned on Tuesday, as it urged the Yemeni rebels to let supplies enter. The fuel crunch is affecting hospitals and putting patients' lives in danger, while many families in Taiz are struggling to obtain water, said Laurent Bukera, a UN humanitarian official in Yemen. The Yemeni government on Tuesday accused the Houthis of firing a mortar shell at an ambulance in Taiz, killing two people including an 18-year-old girl. It said the rebels were carrying out “indiscriminate shelling of residential areas”. The government announced a series of counter-attacks as it tries to regain territory from the Houthis. An offensive by the Iran-backed group in recent weeks has reignited Yemen's civil war and opened a new front in the wider Middle East conflict. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Iran's ambassador to Britain has denied.

"We know the public have unanswered questions," CTP's Taylor said. "I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will."

By Huseyin Hayatsever, Nevzat Devranoglu and Ece Toksabay

ANKARA, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.

The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

The agreement's first article says the parties shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.

"In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them," Article 2 of the agreement says.

The provision, similar to NATO's Article 5, refers to Article 51 of the UNCharter, which covers the individual or collective right of states to self-defence against armed attack.

The three countries "will decide on the scope and nature of the support to be provided following an objective assessment of the assistance required" and will cooperate within their available resources, including military capabilities and resources, the same article says.

At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Turkey, which has a robust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh's military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

The agreement also envisages close cooperation on defence industry, intelligence sharing, logistical support and the fight against "all means of terrorism," includingat the operational level.

Parliamentary ratification is required for Turkey to formally approve the agreement.

AIM TO "STRENGTHEN COLLECTIVE DETERRENCE"

Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, will refer the agreement to parliament's foreign affairs commission upon his return, two of the sources said. The contents and details of the agreement are expected to become public once it is submitted to the commission.

The commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday, another source said.

PresidentTayyip Erdogan's communications director, Burhanettin Duran,said that Turkey's recent step marked an important milestone towards the institutionalisation of strategic cooperation between the three nations.

"This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to strengthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region," Duran said in a post on X.

A Turkish official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Turkey's own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far.

Asked how Turkey could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen'sHouthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Mecca Agreement was not an "offensive agreement," adding that Turkey would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory.

Turkey's constitution requires separate permission from parliament to deploy troops abroad regardless of any international agreement.

singles.headline: Ancient Sudanese workshop sheds light on Kushite royal power
singles.summary: While ancient Egypt dominated the northern Nile Valley, a powerful kingdom emerged farther south in what is now Sudan. Known as Kush, it eventually extended its influence into Egypt, ruling the country during the eighth century BC. Yet despite its political and cultural importance, Kush has received far less archaeological attention than Egypt, and its achievements have often been portrayed as imitations of Egyptian civilisation. Now, archaeologists have uncovered an ancient workshop producing faience, a brightly coloured glazed material, within a major temple complex in the ancient Nubian capital of Napata. The discovery provides new evidence of how Kushite rulers used specialised craft production to reinforce royal authority and control the manufacture of valuable goods. In a study published in the journal Antiquity, researchers from Durham University in the UK and New York University in the US report that the Temple of Sanam, built by Kushite king Taharqo in the seventh century BC, was not simply a place of worship. It also served as a production centre for objects associated with royal power and funerary traditions. “Recent scholarship has increasingly challenged older views that portrayed Kush simply as a copy of Egypt, but important questions remain about how the Kushite state controlled resources, labour, production and the distribution of prestige goods,” said Rennan Lemos, an archaeologist at Durham University and the study’s lead author. A workshop inside a royal temple During excavations at the Sanam temple complex, the research team, working with Kathryn Howley of New York University, discovered the remains of a workshop specialising in faience production, alongside hundreds of faience beads and a small funerary figurine known as a shabti. Shabtis were commonly placed in tombs in ancient Egypt and Nubia. According to funerary beliefs, these small figures could perform work on behalf of the deceased in the afterlife. Faience was also widely used to make jewellery, amulets and decorative objects because of its bright colours and glossy surface, typically in shades of blue, green and white. The material was produced by mixing silica-rich ingredients with other substances and heating the mixture until a glassy layer formed on its surface. In ancient Egypt, faience was associated with brilliance and brightness, reflecting both its appearance and its value. But what particularly interested the researchers was not simply the presence of these objects. It was the location of the workshop itself. Producing faience involved heating materials in a process that generated smoke and unpleasant fumes. In ancient Egypt, workshops carrying out this activity were generally located on the edges of settlements, away from important central areas. At Sanam, however, production took place within a major religious complex, suggesting that the manufacture of valuable objects was closely connected to the institutions supporting royal authority. “This evidence demonstrates that Sanam Temple was not simply a religious monument but also a centre of state-controlled production,” Lemos said. “The workshop produced faience objects associated with royal power, including shabtis destined for the royal cemetery at Nuri.” Nuri was one of the most important royal burial sites in the Kushite kingdom, containing the tombs of several rulers, including Taharqo, who ruled Egypt and Nubia during the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. The discovery therefore offers an unusual glimpse into the economic activities taking place within a royal religious institution and the role of specialised craftspeople in supporting the Kushite state. Nubian innovation rather than Egyptian imitation The workshop also revealed an important difference between the manufacturing techniques used in ancient Egypt and Kush. Egyptian craftspeople commonly used limestone as a source of lime in faience production. But the researchers found evidence suggesting that Kushite artisans may have used crushed seashells instead, an adaptation that made sense because limestone is scarce across much of Sudan. “The workshop reveals Kushite craftspeople adapted Egyptian-inspired technologies to local conditions,” Lemos explained. “Instead of relying on limestone, which is scarce in much of Sudan, they appear to have used crushed seashells as a source of lime in the faience recipe. This points to technological innovation rather than simple imitation.” This finding challenges the long-standing tendency to interpret Kushite material culture primarily through its similarities with ancient Egypt. Although Kushite craftspeople were familiar with Egyptian technologies and artistic traditions, they did not necessarily reproduce them unchanged. Instead, they selected techniques that suited their needs, modified production methods and created objects carrying meanings specific to Kushite society. The researchers argue that the workshop also offers rare physical evidence of how the Kushite state exercised economic and political control. By organising the production of prestigious objects within a royal temple, the authorities may have controlled not only the finished goods but also access to raw materials, skilled labour and the specialised knowledge required to manufacture them. This suggests a possible difference between the economic foundations of royal authority in Egypt and Kush. In ancient Egypt, political and economic power was strongly associated with control over agricultural land and production. The new findings suggest that Kushite rulers also placed considerable importance on controlling the manufacture and distribution of luxury and ceremonial objects. However, the discovery provides direct evidence from one royal temple complex rather than a complete picture of the Kushite economy. It does not establish that all craft production across the kingdom was organised in the same way. For Lemos, the significance of the findings extends beyond the workshop itself. “This highlights the creativity and agency of ancient Nubian societies,” he said. Rather than simply adopting Egyptian cultural practices, the Kushites adapted foreign technologies to local circumstances, developed their own production methods and created objects with distinct political and social meanings. The discovery at Sanam adds an important dimension to the history of Kush, showing that temples could function as centres of economic production as well as religious worship. It also reveals how the artisans who made beads, ornaments and funerary figures contributed to the political authority of one of the Nile Valley’s most influential ancient civilisations.

singles.headline: Robots and AI could make smart farming profitable on 75% of global cropland: Study
singles.summary: Drones that detect crop pests, robots that remove weeds and artificial intelligence (AI) systems that determine where to apply water and fertilizer are becoming increasingly common on farms. These technologies promise to cut costs and reduce environmental damage, but their economic benefits vary widely. Where does investing in smart farming actually pay off? A new international study led by researchers at the University of Bonn in Germany finds that smart farming technologies are already economically viable on around 42% of the world’s cropland. That share could rise to 50% over the next two decades and reach 75% if countries strengthen their environmental regulations. If governments weaken those rules, however, the proportion could fall to just 31%. Published on 19 October in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the study provides a global assessment of where smart farming technologies can be profitable. It also identifies regions where their adoption could help address pressing environmental challenges, including water scarcity and excessive fertilizer use. “These smart farming technologies have the potential to make crop farming more sustainable and environmentally friendly,” says David Wuepper, a professor at the University of Bonn and one of the study’s lead researchers. However, he cautions that adopting these technologies does not automatically make financial sense for every farm. High upfront costs and the technical expertise required to operate the equipment can make investment difficult, particularly in the short term. Where does smart farming pay off? Across Europe and North America, farmers are increasingly using drones to detect pest infestations and target pesticide applications more precisely. Robots can remove weeds before they spread, while automated irrigation systems monitor soil moisture and direct water to where it is needed. By reducing unnecessary applications of water, fertilizers and pesticides, these technologies can lower operating costs and limit environmental harm. Their economic value, however, depends on local conditions, including farm size, labour costs, education levels and environmental regulations. To assess these differences, the researchers consulted more than 8,000 smart farming experts worldwide, asking them to identify locations where these technologies were already being used profitably. They also reviewed scientific studies documenting real-world applications. The team compiled data from more than 4,000 locations where technologies such as automated irrigation, weeding robots and drone-based monitoring were in use. They then applied machine-learning methods to identify the factors associated with profitable adoption. The results point to the strongest economic potential in regions with higher incomes, better education systems, larger farms and stricter environmental regulations. These include Western Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia. Shahrear Roman, a doctoral researcher in Wuepper’s group, explains that farms in these regions often use substantial quantities of fertilizers and pesticides. Precision technologies can help farmers cut costs by applying these products only where they are needed. Higher labour costs also make automation more attractive, improving the financial case for investing in robots and automated machinery. The outlook is different in sub-Saharan Africa, where the economic potential of smart farming remains comparatively limited, despite the need to improve agricultural productivity and resource management. One major obstacle, Wuepper says, is that many existing technologies have been designed for large, capital-intensive farms in Europe and North America. As a result, they may be poorly suited to smaller agricultural operations. “At the moment, the equipment is being developed with a focus on large, capital-intensive operations in North America and Europe,” he says. Wuepper argues that agricultural research and development should place greater emphasis on affordable technologies tailored to smallholder farmers. Such innovations could help extend the benefits of smart farming beyond wealthier agricultural regions. Environmental policies could reshape the market One of the study’s most striking findings is the role of environmental governance in determining where smart farming becomes profitable. The researchers found that the strength of environmental regulations was the most important predictor of profitability in their models, outweighing the other factors they examined. “We found that smart farming already pays off where environmental governance is strongest. It is by far the most important predictor in our models,” Roman says. Combining these findings with regional economic forecasts, the team developed a global assessment of where smart farming technologies could become economically viable over the coming decades. The analysis covered five technology categories: automated irrigation systems; weeding robots; drones and other field-monitoring tools; machinery that automatically adjusts fertilizer and pesticide applications; and GPS-guided equipment that reduces overlapping passes across fields. The researchers also examined where profitable adoption could coincide with substantial environmental benefits, identifying regions where the economic case for smart farming overlaps with pressing ecological challenges. Smart irrigation, for example, was often found to be economically attractive in areas facing growing water shortages. This suggests that farmers in these regions could potentially reduce water use while improving their financial performance. The findings also highlight how policy choices could influence investment. Stronger environmental regulations could expand the share of global cropland where smart farming is profitable, while weaker rules could undermine incentives to adopt the technologies. These figures are scenario-based estimates, not guaranteed forecasts. The actual expansion of smart farming will depend on economic development, government policies, access to technology and farmers’ ability to finance new equipment. “Ecological and economic benefits often go hand in hand. But they do not arrive on their own: without policy, most of the environmental gain stays on the table,” Wuepper says. Ultimately, the future of smart farming will depend on more than advances in robotics, drones and AI. It will also hinge on whether governments, researchers and technology developers can make these tools affordable and practical for a wider range of farmers. That challenge is particularly important for smallholders, who often face limited access to finance and technology even as they contend with water scarcity, rising input costs and pressure to improve productivity.

It also identifies regions where their adoption could help address pressing environmental challenges, including water scarcity and excessive fertilizer use.

“These smart farming technologies have the potential to make crop farming more sustainable and environmentally friendly,” says David Wuepper, a professor at the University of Bonn and one of the study’s lead researchers.

However, he cautions that adopting these technologies does not automatically make financial sense for every farm. High upfront costs and the technical expertise required to operate the equipment can make investment difficult, particularly in the short term.

Where does smart farming pay off?

Across Europe and North America, farmers are increasingly using drones to detect pest infestations and target pesticide applications more precisely. Robots can remove weeds before they spread, while automated irrigation systems monitor soil moisture and direct water to where it is needed.

By reducing unnecessary applications of water, fertilizers and pesticides, these technologies can lower operating costs and limit environmental harm. Their economic value, however, depends on local conditions, including farm size, labour costs, education levels and environmental regulations.

To assess these differences, the researchers consulted more than 8,000 smart farming experts worldwide, asking them to identify locations where these technologies were already being used profitably. They also reviewed scientific studies documenting real-world applications.

The team compiled data from more than 4,000 locations where technologies such as automated irrigation, weeding robots and drone-based monitoring were in use. They then applied machine-learning methods to identify the factors associated with profitable adoption.

The results point to the strongest economic potential in regions with higher incomes, better education systems, larger farms and stricter environmental regulations. These include Western Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia.

Shahrear Roman, a doctoral researcher in Wuepper’s group, explains that farms in these regions often use substantial quantities of fertilizers and pesticides. Precision technologies can help farmers cut costs by applying these products only where they are needed.

Higher labour costs also make automation more attractive, improving the financial case for investing in robots and automated machinery.

The outlook is different in sub-Saharan Africa, where the economic potential of smart farming remains comparatively limited, despite the need to improve agricultural productivity and resource management.

One major obstacle, Wuepper says, is that many existing technologies have been designed for large, capital-intensive farms in Europe and North America. As a result, they may be poorly suited to smaller agricultural operations.

“At the moment, the equipment is being developed with a focus on large, capital-intensive operations in North America and Europe,” he says.

Wuepper argues that agricultural research and development should place greater emphasis on affordable technologies tailored to smallholder farmers. Such innovations could help extend the benefits of smart farming beyond wealthier agricultural regions.

Environmental policies could reshape the market

One of the study’s most striking findings is the role of environmental governance in determining where smart farming becomes profitable.

The researchers found that the strength of environmental regulations was the most important predictor of profitability in their models, outweighing the other factors they examined.

“We found that smart farming already pays off where environmental governance is strongest. It is by far the most important predictor in our models,” Roman says.

Combining these findings with regional economic forecasts, the team developed a global assessment of where smart farming technologies could become economically viable over the coming decades.

The analysis covered five technology categories: automated irrigation systems; weeding robots; drones and other field-monitoring tools; machinery that automatically adjusts fertilizer and pesticide applications; and GPS-guided equipment that reduces overlapping passes across fields.

The researchers also examined where profitable adoption could coincide with substantial environmental benefits, identifying regions where the economic case for smart farming overlaps with pressing ecological challenges.

Smart irrigation, for example, was often found to be economically attractive in areas facing growing water shortages. This suggests that farmers in these regions could potentially reduce water use while improving their financial performance.

The findings also highlight how policy choices could influence investment. Stronger environmental regulations could expand the share of global cropland where smart farming is profitable, while weaker rules could undermine incentives to adopt the technologies.

These figures are scenario-based estimates, not guaranteed forecasts. The actual expansion of smart farming will depend on economic development, government policies, access to technology and farmers’ ability to finance new equipment.

“Ecological and economic benefits often go hand in hand. But they do not arrive on their own: without policy, most of the environmental gain stays on the table,” Wuepper says.

Ultimately, the future of smart farming will depend on more than advances in robotics, drones and AI. It will also hinge on whether governments, researchers and technology developers can make these tools affordable and practical for a wider range of farmers. That challenge is particularly important for smallholders, who often face limited access to finance and technology even as they contend with water scarcity, rising input costs and pressure to improve productivity.
