singles.headline: Cairo hosts UfM Economic Forum to strengthen regional investment, trade
singles.summary: Cairo hosted the Economic Forum of the Union for the Mediterranean (UfM) from October 19 to 22, bringing together government representatives, private-sector leaders and development partners to explore ways to strengthen regional investment, expand trade and create jobs across the Euro-Mediterranean region. Held in cooperation with the European Union and with support from the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), the forum focused on improving the business environment, enhancing economic competitiveness and strengthening the role of companies in driving sustainable and inclusive growth. The opening session was attended by European Union Ambassador to Egypt Angelina Eichhorst, Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to Egypt Jürgen Schulz, UfM Senior Deputy Secretary-General Mariam Diallo, and CEO of the Grand Egyptian Museum Ahmed Ghoneim. UfM Deputy Secretary-General for Economic Development and Employment Meltem Büyükkarakaş also attended. The forum coincided with a meeting between Fadi Haj Ali, Acting Secretary-General of the UfM, and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty to discuss regional developments and preparations for the organisation’s 11th Regional Forum, scheduled to take place in Barcelona next month. UfM Senior Deputy Secretary-General Mariam Diallo said the event reaffirmed the UfM’s commitment to regional economic integration, trade and investment facilitation, and stronger and more sustainable partnerships across the Mediterranean. She stressed that investment extends beyond capital flows and project development to include investment in human capabilities, innovation and production, which are essential to building more prosperous and stable societies. UfM Deputy Secretary-General for Economic Development and Employment Meltem Büyükkarakaş welcomed Egypt’s hosting of the forum, saying Cairo provided a platform to advance regional dialogue towards practical partnerships that could expand investment, production and export opportunities for businesses in Egypt and other Mediterranean countries. She highlighted the importance of simplifying procedures and improving access to finance and markets, in cooperation with the private sector, to translate regional opportunities into sustainable growth and employment. European Union Ambassador to Egypt Angelina Eichhorst underlined the need to deepen economic integration between the two shores of the Mediterranean, arguing that the region should increasingly function as an integrated economic space connecting businesses, investment, value chains and people. She noted that the European Union accounts for 42.1% of the region’s total exports, making it the region’s leading trading partner by a significant margin. However, she said substantial opportunities for further economic cooperation remain untapped. Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to Egypt Jürgen Schulz said trust was the main driver of investment and that coordinated efforts could turn reforms into investment and employment opportunities. He reaffirmed Germany’s commitment to working with European partners in support of regional development. High-level sessions examined regulatory reforms, streamlined procedures and measures to facilitate trade and investment. Discussions also explored opportunities in regional value chains, the digital economy and information and communications technology, alongside ways to strengthen public-private partnerships and attract sustainable investment. The forum’s programme included workshops and capacity-building sessions on digital trade, e-commerce and cross-border transactions, as well as the revised regional convention on pan-Euro-Mediterranean preferential rules of origin and its implementation. The conclusions and recommendations from the discussions will be compiled into policy briefs to support regional economic-development dialogue and help inform implementation of the European Union’s Pact for the Mediterranean. The event also provided a business-to-business networking platform designed to help companies arrange meetings and develop partnerships during and after the forum.

ANKARA/TORONTO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - NATO allies Canada and Turkey are expected to sign a joint declaration aimed at deepening bilateral cooperation in four areas, including defence and energy, during Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit later this week, a person briefed on the matter said.

The declaration is also expected to encompass the economy, looking to advance free trade talks between the countries, while boosting social and diplomatic ties. The countries would establish committees in all of the areas to draft action plans, the person said.

Carney's office and Turkey's presidency and Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Carney will be the first Canadian prime minister to make a dedicated bilateral visit to Turkey. He is set to meet with Turkish PresidentTayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Thursday and is expected to meet with Turkish business leaders in Istanbul on Friday.

The visit is part of Carney's effortsto reduce trade dependence on the United States and strengthen partnerships with regional powers amid a damaging trade war with Washington and an increasingly adversarial relationship with President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly questioned Canada's sovereignty.

TALKS MAY INCLUDE NUCLEAR POWER, LNG

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar told the Kanal 7 broadcaster on Sunday that energy, namely nuclear power, would be among the top agenda items during Carney’s visit.

Ankara anticipates that energy discussions will also include potential purchases by Turkey of liquefied natural gas from Canada as well as critical minerals, the person said. A working group is expected to be created to study the feasibility of a bid by Canada's CANDU to build a planned nuclear plant on Turkey's Black Sea coast.

Turkey has held talks with Canadian engineering firmAtkinsRealis ATRL.TO, which owns CANDU, as well as South Korea's ​Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation, about potentially building its planned second and third nuclear power plants. Russia's Rosatom is ⁠building its first.

The discussions on the defence sector are expected to focus on drones and naval cooperation. In 2024, to help thaw bilateral ties, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkey, including on optical ​technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of nations.

Carney is also expected to meet with officials from defence companies as well as firms with energy businesses during his visit to Turkey, including Calik Holding and Sabanci Holding, according to two otherpeople familiar with the plans. Sabanci Holding declined to comment while Calik Holding did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Turkish defence analysts said Trump's policies towards Canada had created opportunities for closer cooperation in ammunition production, drones and naval systems, but cautioned that major agreements were unlikely tomaterialise in the short term.

(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu in Ankara and Jonathan Spicer in Toronto, Additional reporting by Ece Toksabay, Maria Cheng in Ottawa, Can Sezer and Ebru Tuncay in Istanbul and Huseyin Hayatsever in Ankara, Writing by Humeyra Pamuk, Editing by Daren Butler and Rod Nickel)

singles.body_text:
The three-day exhibition brings together international security companies and officials, with Qatar and France signing a new security cooperation plan. The 16th edition of Milipol Qatar opened at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Center (DECC) on Tuesday, bringing together more than 270 local and international companies showcasing the latest technologies, law enforcement authorities, security agencies and industry representatives to exchange expertise and explore partnerships as security challenges continue to evolve.

Held under the patronage of Qatar’s Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, the exhibition runs from 20 to 22 October, featuring seven international pavilions across 23,000 square metres of exhibition space.

Qatar’s Minister of Interior and Commander of the Internal Security Force (Lekhwiya), Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani, attended the opening and toured the exhibition alongside senior officials.

Minister of State for Interior Affairs Sheikh Abdulaziz bin Faisal bin Mohammed Al Thani also toured the exhibition, where he was briefed on the latest security technologies, products and systems presented by participating companies.

Organised by Qatar’s Ministry of Interior, Milipol Qatar has been held every two years since 1996, serving as a platform for security agencies, government officials and international companies to explore emerging technologies and strengthen cooperation.

The parties will also cooperate in the areas of security, intelligence, and counterterrorism. The pact’s strategic, political, and defense committees, which will include foreign and defense ministers, and chiefs of staff, will meet at least twice a year on a rotating basis, while the countries’ leaders will meet once a year if they deem it necessary, according to excerpts from the document cited by the TRT Haber television channel.

The United Nations insisted Tuesday that aid must immediately be allowed to enter Yemen's Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching the country's third-largest city.

Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognised government.

"Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated," UN human rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.

He said relief must reach the city to avert a rights catastrophe.

"The Houthis' closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies," said Turk.

The Houthis, from Yemen's rugged north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, sparking a brutal civil war with a Saudi-led coalition fighting for the government.

The civil war reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.

Turk said the encirclement of Taiz had sent the prices of commodities soaring, leaving many without food or other basic necessities.

His office has also noted restrictions on safe access to water and essential goods, exacerbating humanitarian needs and increasing risks for civilians.

"Civilians wishing to leave must be allowed to do so freely and safely," said Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights.

Turk's office said it had verified that 32 civilians had been killed across Taiz governorate between August 1 and October 19, including nine women and 14 children.

Meanwhile 115 civilians were injured, among them 34 women and 36 children.

Turk warned that with fighting moving closer to densely populated areas of the city, the risk of death and injury to civilians would only increase.

"I urge all parties to the conflict to refrain from the use of explosive weapons with wide-area effects in populated areas and to take all feasible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects," he said.

The World Health Organization said that Taiz's health system was now at "critical risk".

"Fighting and road closures are threatening hospitals' access to fuel, oxygen, medicines and essential supplies, putting patients requiring life-saving care at immediate risk," WHO spokesman Tarik Jasarevic told a press conference.

The UN health agency is calling for the safe movement of patients, health workers, ambulances, fuel, oxygen and medicines to the city.

Jasarevic said 12 hospitals in Taiz had around four days of fuel left, while there are stocks of one week or less for 115 out of 127 essential medicines.

He said the health crisis across Yemen was escalating rapidly, with rising disease outbreaks placing "immense pressure on an already overstretched health system".

Across Yemen, suspected cholera cases have tripled from 221 in the week ending September 12 to 683 in the week ending October 10.

Yemen has reported this year more than 22,800 suspected measles cases and 128 deaths, alongside 12,618 suspected dengue cases and 421 suspected diphtheria cases.

singles.summary: With airports closed and the capital brought to an effective standstill, attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia have thrown a wrench in the kingdom's ambitious plans to overhaul the economy and draw foreign investment. singles.body_text:
With airports closed and the capital brought to an effective standstill, attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia have thrown a wrench in the kingdom's ambitious plans to overhaul the economy and draw foreign investment.

A decade ago, de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman launched his bold Vision 2030, aiming to diversify the economy away from oil and turn the powerful monarchy into a hub for tourism, international events and multinational enterprises.

Already dealt a blow by Iran's attacks on US allies in the Gulf during the wider Middle East war, the plan now faces an existential hurdle with unprecedented Houthi attacks, in particular targeting oil infrastructure and airports.

"I can't think of another time when the challenge facing MBS was more," said H.A. Hellyer, an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

"He's dealing with the Iranians on one side of the country which is very difficult and problematic and then he's dealing with the Houthis who aligned with the Iranians on the other."

On October 10, a Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300 -- the deadliest in the kingdom in over a decade, with the airport remaining closed since.

A consultant to the Saudi government who wished to remain anonymous meanwhile told AFP that "the deeper risk there is that, you know, boards start pricing Saudi as part of an active conflict zone.

"If that perception settles into risk models, insurance premiums, it will take many years to unwind," she added.

A number of major events have been cancelled, most notably the Future Investment Initiative (FII), nicknamed "Davos on the desert" -- a bulwark of the kingdom's diversification drive.

The uncertainty has only piled pressure on the 41-year-old crown prince's Vision 2030, as several of its megaprojects -- most notably the hyper-futuristic megacity dubbed Neom -- have been scaled back.

In Riyadh, the iconic Kingdom Centre recently ordered its office tenants, which include the International Monetary Fund (IMF), to work remotely until further notice.

The world's largest crude oil exporter is moreover expected to see its economy contract by 3.3 percent, according to the IMF's latest projections, revised from a projected growth of 1.7 percent in July.

The kingdom is grappling with a new reality wherein US protection is no longer guaranteed, as President Donald Trump has appeared reluctant to offer support in Yemen as he gears up for mid-term elections.

"Saudi Arabia finds itself in a delicate situation in the face of Houthi attacks, as well as US hesitation," said Laurent Bonnefoy, a researcher at Ceri/Sciences Po in Paris.

"Trump for the time being seems to be refusing to commit to offering the needed military backing," he added.

Riyadh has secured support from several allies including France, Britain, Turkey and Pakistan to help mitigate the threat posed by the Houthis," said Torbjorn Soltvedt, Middle East analyst at Verisk Maplecroft.

"But all are reluctant to go beyond defensive measures, with no appetite to put troops on the ground in Yemen."

The Houthis for their part are relying on a vast arsenal of weapons built up over years with Iranian support.

Following an uneasy four-year truce in the war, fighting kicked off again in July when the airport in Sanaa was struck after Iran sent a plane in defiance of Saudi control -- an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia.

The Yemeni group has a large number of longer-range missiles and drones at its disposal, and has seized control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which leads up to the Suez Canal.

After pursuing a policy of "power and regional projection" in 2019, Riyadh -- facing a "stalemate" in Yemen -- shifted tack around 2019 and focused on economic objectives, Bonnefoy said.

Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst close to the Saudi government, said the kingdom "has faced repeated challenges over the decades".

"The Kingdom has weathered each crisis and will weather this one. It is resilient, has staying power and can draw on global supply chains and an extensive network of alliances," he said.

"The Houthis, ultimately, have only Iran, and Iran itself is under severe strain."

But Soltvedt suggested the risks predate the latest conflict, saying: "Allaying investor concerns over geopolitical risk has been a longstanding challenge for Riyadh, from the attacks on the heart of Saudi Arabia's energy sector just before the Aramco IPO in 2019, to the outbreak of regional conflict this year.

"With no solution to the conflict in sight, the drone and missile threat from multiple directions and actors will continue to weigh on the minds of investors."

singles.headline: Africa: TotalEnergies CAF Futsal Afcon - Hornes Santo - 'We Never Give Up'
singles.summary: [CAF] Angola's Palancas Negras produced a stunning second-half comeback to overturn a two-goal deficit and beat Algeria 3-2 in the semi-finals of the TotalEnergies CAF Futsal Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2026. The result sends the 2024 runners-up into a second consecutive final.
singles.body_text:
Angola's Palancas Negras produced a stunning second-half comeback to overturn a two-goal deficit and beat Algeria 3-2 in the semi-finals of the TotalEnergies CAF Futsal Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2026. The result sends the 2024 runners-up into a second consecutive final.

Algeria, playing in their first semi-final at their first tournament, made life difficult for the Angolans. The spirited debutants went ahead through Mathieu Hammad and Ait Hamadouce, leaving the Palancas Negras with a mountain to climb.

Angola did not panic, Aderito Santos pulled one back to restore belief, and the momentum began to shift toward the side that had been here before.

Hornes Santo then drew Angola level five minutes from time, completing the recovery from 2-0 down. With extra time and penalties looming, Francisco Chico settled it two minutes from the end with a clever finish.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

For Hornes, the equalizer capped an emotional night. "First of all, I thank God for everything he has done in my life," he told CAFOnline. "It was a wonderful feeling. I'm so happy, I can't explain what I'm feeling right now."

Asked what makes this Angolan side so hard to beat, he pointed to belief. "We never give up. We always believe. The game only finishes when the clock reaches zero, and if we have to go to penalties, we'll believe, game by game."

Angola now have a chance to go one better than their runners-up finish in 2024, when they lost the final to Morocco. For Hornes, this is the first final. "I'm here to become a champion," he said. "I'm not here to visit Morocco, I'm here to compete. This is my time."

Ait Hamadouche: "We lacked experience, but I am proud of the boys"

Meanwhile, Algeria's Ait Hamadouche said he's proud of his team despite losing the chance to reach the final.

The Algerian ace played a key role on the night at the Salle Moulay Abdellah in Rabat on Monday. Mathieu Hammad put the Fennecs ahead with a stunning free kick after nine minutes, and Ait Hamadouche doubled the lead on the stroke of halftime.

Speaking to CAFOnline after the match, he said the first half had gone as planned. "We had a good first half and took a 1-0 lead, but we knew our opponents well," he said. "They are used to coming back from behind."

That proved accurate as Angola returned from the break with renewed momentum, and Aderito Santos pulled one back from close range midway through the second period. Hornes Santo then levelled on 35 minutes, and Francisco Gabriel struck the winner two minutes from time.

singles.headline: Brazil's Newcastle poultry outbreak unlikely to have major long-term impact, analysts say
singles.summary: By Gabriel AraujoSAO PAULO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - An outbreak of Newcastle disease in Brazil is unlikely to cause lasting damage to the country's poultry industry if authorities contain it quickly, analysts said, though uncertainty over trade restrictions, particularly from China, remains a key risk for exporters.Brazil, the world's largest chicken meat exporter, confirmed a case of the disease at a commercial farm in the southern state of Santa Catarina on Monday, prompting containment measures and triggering concerns over poultry trade flows.
singles.body_text:
SAO PAULO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - An outbreak of Newcastle disease in Brazil is unlikely to cause lasting damage to the country's poultry industry if authorities contain it quickly, analysts said, though uncertainty over trade restrictions, particularly from China, remains a key risk for exporters.

Brazil, the world's largest chicken meat exporter, confirmed a case of the disease at a commercial farm in the southern state of Santa Catarina on Monday, prompting containment measures and triggering concerns over poultry trade flows.

Mexico, Brazil's seventh-largest poultry buyer last year, quickly suspended imports, while meat lobby group ABPA said Brazil would impose a self-embargo on shipments to China pending a decision by Chinese authorities on whether restrictions would apply nationwide or only to the affected area.

Shares in major poultry processor MBRF fell more than 4% on Monday, while US-traded peer JBS slipped 1%.

Brazil last reported a Newcastle disease outbreak in July 2024 in Rio Grande do Sul state, which neighbors Santa Catarina.

Chicken exports fell by about 25%, or 100,000 metric tons, during the month affected by restrictions that year, analysts at JPMorgan estimated, but rebounded quickly as markets reopened, causing no material effect on MBRF'sand JBS' earnings.

China was the most consequential source of trade disruption as it kept a state-wide embargo in place until January 2026, they noted, but other key destinations such as Mexico, the European Union, Saudi Arabia and Japan either eased restrictions quickly or implemented a localized response.

"This time around, unless we see a widespread event happening (which is unusual for this disease), we think the impact could be even smaller as several countries have changed their restriction protocol to a radius," JPMorgan said.

Santander analysts also flagged China -- which currently accounts for roughly 10% of Brazilian chicken exports -- as the key uncertainty, adding that MBRF is more exposed than geographically diversified JBS to potential disruptions.

They estimated trade restrictions could affect about 15% of Brazil's chicken production under current export protocols.

Prolonged restrictions could force exporters to redirect shipments to alternative markets or the domestic market, potentially weighing on prices and margins, Santander said.

"All in all, we are monitoring the scope and duration of trade restrictions. Lack of visibility on the duration of Chinese suspension is the key risk," they added.

(Reporting by Gabriel Araujo; Editing by Oliver Griffin and Alistair Bell)

singles.body_text:
The UAE's response to an attack on the Barakah nuclear plant in May was swift and effective, the International Atomic Energy Agency has concluded.

A drone launched from Iraq struck a generator outside the inner perimeter of the Barakah plant, causing a fire that was brought under control.

Dozens of countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, the UK, the US, France and Pakistan, as well as the EU, signed a statement condemning the attack.

UN Security Council condemns drone strike on UAE's Barakah nuclear power plant

The IAEA concluded on Tuesday that national authorities and Barakah Nuclear Power Plant had appropriately responded to the loss of off-site power due to the drone strike on May 17.

The finding was reached by a six-person mission team from the nuclear agency who were in the UAE from October 12 to October 20 at the request of the government.

Effective action was taken to maintain safety during the event, including prompt national and international notification, implementation of the established emergency response procedures, and public communication, the IAEA said in a statement.

Its team visited the affected areas of the plant and key emergency response facilities, reviewed operating and emergency procedures, and met the senior management and technical staff of BNPP and the Federal Authority for Nuclear Regulation (FANR), the UAE’s independent nuclear regulator.

The team focused on plant response actions, national arrangements for emergency preparedness and response, lessons learnt from the incident, and the reactor operator’s arrangements to ensure safety, the statement added.

“By requesting this mission, FANR and BNPP have demonstrated their strong commitment to safety and continuous improvement,” said Amgad Shokr, director of the IAEA Incident and Emergency Centre and leader of the mission team.

Barakah Nuclear Power Plant was “encouraged to continue implementing the organisational and technical measures identified through the assessment of lessons learnt from the event”.

“The UAE has established a robust and comprehensive nuclear emergency preparedness and response system in line with the highest international standards, developed in close co-operation with the IAEA,” said Hamad Al Kaabi, director general of FANR.

“The UAE shares the position of the international community and the IAEA on the importance of protecting nuclear facilities at all times. We will continue working closely with the IAEA and our national partners to enhance the safety and security of nuclear facilities and ensure the protection of the community and the environment.”

singles.headline: Turkey troops to stay in Syria, Iraq 'until border security ensured', defence minister tells AFP
singles.summary: Turkey will keep its own troops in Syria and Iraq until border security with its two neighbours has been fully ensured, Defence Minister Yasar Guler told AFP. "We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria," he said in a written answer to AFP questions. "When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered."
singles.body_text:
Turkey will keep its own troops in Syria and Iraq until border security with its two neighbours has been fully ensured, Defence Minister Yasar Guler told AFP.

"We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria," he said in a written answer to AFP questions.

"When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered."

Turkey has for years maintained troops in northern Syria and Iraq to contain the threat along its borders posed by separatist militants from the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) and from Islamic State (IS) jihadists.

But over the past two years, the situation has shifted with the emergence of a new Ankara-allied government in Syria following Bashar al-Assad's fall, and following Turkey's push to draw a line under its decades-long conflict with the PKK.

Since Assad's fall, Turkey had established "close coordination in the field of security" with the new Syrian government, with its troops working to "strengthen the capacity" of the Syrian military and "to ensure the security of our borders", the minister said.

"Once the terrorist threat in the region has been completely eliminated, border security has been ensured, and state authority has been fully and uniformly established throughout Syria without exception, the status of our forces will be reassessed," he said.

When the Assad regime fell, Turkey had between 16,000 and 18,000 troops in northern Syria, a Turkish official said.

Since then, there has been no reliable figure for troops deployed in Syria, although a Turkish official last month said talks were under way to determine their legal status there.

But Guler refused to be drawn on any future plans.

"At this stage it would not be appropriate to make a prior assessment regarding deployment or base plans that have not been made public," he said.

"Issues related to the future posture of the Turkish armed forces in Syria will be addressed by taking into account Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, the mutual understanding of the two countries, the security conditions on the ground and the evolution of the terrorist threat."

Turkish troops have also long been operational in northern Iraq, regularly conducting cross-border operations and air raids on PKK hideouts, while maintaining their own bases there -- putting a strain on ties between Ankara and Baghdad.

Troops have been based there since 2015, and today they number between 800 and 1,000, an Iraqi security source told AFP.

Without disclosing any figures, Guler said troop numbers in both Iraq and Syria were assessed in proportion to what was needed on the ground.

"It would not be accurate to assess our military presence in Iraq and Syria solely on the basis of personnel numbers. Our force structure and posture on the ground are shaped according to needs" linked to threat levels, border security and developments on the ground, he said.

As the PKK process has advanced, the Kurdish militants destroyed weapons at a symbolic ceremony last year, and this month, withdrew from four key bases in northern Iraq in a move confirmed by Turkish intelligence.

For lasting success, the PKK must "fully implement their decision to dissolve" with Turkey "meticulously monitoring the next phases of the process" while not dropping its guard.

"The progress of the process doesn't mean security measures have been relaxed," he said, with troops continuing to "take the necessary measures" against any situation viewed as a security threat.

Like in Syria, Turkey was also closely watching Iraq's own efforts "to disarm militia groups and bring them under state control", he said, hailing recent successes in the Sinjar region.

Iraq has set a June 30 deadline for pro-Iran factions to hand over their weapons to the state following the end of the US-led coalition's mission there.

Following the successful Sinjar push, Turkey said last month it would "gradually" hand control to Baghdad of its Bashiqa base near the northern city of Mosul although no timeline was given.

Turkey would continue to support Iraq and was planning "to elevate military and security cooperation between the two countries to a higher level" in the coming period, he said.

singles.headline: Qatar warns Hormuz cable disruption would hit region hardest, urges peaceful U.S.-Iran resolution
singles.summary: During Tuesday’s weekly press briefing at MoFA, Ibrahim Al Hashmi said that countries across the region rely on the Strait of Hormuz’s waters for irrigation, salt production and fisheries, warning…
singles.body_text:
During Tuesday’s weekly press briefing at MoFA, Ibrahim Al Hashmi said that countries across the region rely on the Strait of Hormuz’s waters for irrigation, salt production and fisheries, warning that damage could threaten water security.

Qatar has said any disruption to undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz would affect countries across the region, including Iran, and called for attacks and threats targeting the waterway to stop immediately.

Ibrahim Al Hashmi, director of the Media and Communications Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA), said at Tuesday’s weekly press briefing that countries in the region, including Iran, would bear the greatest impact of any disruption to undersea cables.

“If someone on the Iranian side reflected honestly on the situation, they would ask: who is the biggest victim?” Al Hashmi asserted.

The MoFA spokesperson added that neither the United States nor Israel would suffer the greatest impact, but countries across the region, including Iran.

“Will it be the United States? Will it be Israel, which does not benefit from the Gulf’s waters? Or will it be the countries in the region, including the Iranian people?”

The remarks follow an earlier warning from Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, who warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the region could be attacked if war with the United States erupts again.

The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia.

Fighting is under way between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis at several locations, including Bab al-Mandeb, through which nearly one-fifth of global internet traffic passes.

Al Hashmi said countries across the region rely on the Strait of Hormuz’s waters for irrigation, salt production and fisheries, warning that damage could threaten water security.

“Water security in the Strait of Hormuz is an integral part of water security for our region and our people,” he said, adding that Iran had a responsibility to protect the waters, uphold international law on freedom of navigation and preserve the marine environment.

He called for the “irresponsible attacks” to stop immediately, warning that they harmed people across the region.

Al Hashmi reiterated Qatar’s commitment to mediating the US-Iran crisis, stressing that a peaceful resolution is the only way to preserve regional stability.

He said mediators must remain optimistic and continue working tirelessly to reach an agreement as soon as possible.

“We hope that the solution will be tomorrow, or today, as soon as possible,” Al Hashmi said. “Therefore, we must remain optimistic and work tirelessly and relentlessly to reach a solution.”

Al Hashmi said it was unacceptable for mediators to give in to despair or consider military action a viable solution, warning against further escalation.

“We must be focused on a peaceful solution at the negotiating table,” he said. “It is the only solution that preserves the region and its stability. And we must work towards that with every possible effort.”

They signed an intergovernmental agreement for co-operation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within the French and Emirati Rafale programmes during the visit of French President Emmanuel Macron to Abu Dhabi.

The agreements also cover technical and financial specifications for industrial co-operation between the two countries on the future of combat aviation, as France and the UAE strengthen defence ties.

France seeks stronger UAE ties before investment event in Paris

Another agreement focuses on strategic autonomy in defence and reducing dependence on third countries as part of a strategic defence partnership between the two nations.

The latest agreements come as the UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, focuses on localising defence manufacturing through Edge Group, a defence conglomerate with more than 35 companies under its umbrella.

The group has played a key role in countering Iranian drones directed at the UAE during the war.

Mr Macron visited an Edge Group industrial site during his visit.

Edge, set up in 2019, specialises in developing advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare.

The group maintains several industrial partnerships with French companies and recently signed a co-operation agreement with the French Defence Procurement Agency.

Mr Macron's visit “reflects a shared commitment to strengthening industrial and technological co-operation and developing joint projects”, the Elysee Palace said in a statement.

The French Defence Ministry also signed an agreement with the UAE to enhance interoperability between the two armed forces, strengthen industrial resilience and advance co-operation in future-orientated technology, including artificial intelligence and space.

The latest agreements come as Abu Dhabi is preparing to host the International Defence Exhibition and Conference (Idex) in January, an event expected to attract hundreds of defence companies from across the globe to showcase their latest high-tech weapons.

Mr Macron then headed to Bahrain, where French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif Al Zayani, agreed to bolster co-operation on the “peaceful uses of nuclear energy”, the French government said.

France and Bahrain signed a defence co-operation agreement in February during a visit to Paris by Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa. The UAE and Bahrain were among the Gulf countries France helped protect with air defence and anti-drone assets during Iranian attacks this year.

France has also co-operated closely with Bahrain at the UN Security Council to find a diplomatic solution to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

The UAE and France signed new deals in energy, AI and advanced technology as the two countries seek to strengthen investment and economic ties.

The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in Abu Dhabi.

In his opening remarks at the UAE-France Business Dialogue at Qasr Al Watan in Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled underscored the importance of bilateral co-operation in ensuring reliable energy supplies and building resilient supply chains amid changes in the global economy.

The UAE and France have strong economic ties, with more than 600 French businesses currently operating in the UAE and $4 billion worth of goods exported annually from France to the UAE, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website.

UAE investments are also growing in France. In 2021, UAE-based Gulf Islamic Investments made a $301 million investment in Altais Towers, while Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment Company signed an initial agreement with Bpifrance, committing to invest €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in the LAC1 Fund, a €10 billion fund managed by Bpifrance.

Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has reopened, but travel to the Saudi capital remains disrupted, with selected flights on the schedule alongside cancellations and diversions.

Flightradar24’s arrivals and departures boards for Tuesday show services scheduled by Saudi carriers Saudia, Riyadh Air, flynas and flyadeal alongside some international airlines such as Air Cairo and ITA Airways.

Domestic flights continue, with services listed to destinations including Jeddah, Dammam and Abha. However, cancellations have affected some Saudi-operated flights as well as international connections.

Riyadh airport reopens: Which airlines are still flying to Saudi Arabia?

For passengers planning to travel to Riyadh, here’s what to know.

Saudi carriers have several services to Dubai listed on the departures board, including Riyadh Air flight RX243, flynas flights XY207 and XY211, and Saudia flight SV560.

Air Arabia’s flights between Sharjah and Riyadh remain cancelled, with the airline yet to announce a date for their resumption.

Other UAE connections are also marked as cancelled, including Emirates flight EK820 and flydubai flight FZ848 from Riyadh to Dubai, alongside Etihad Airways flight EY556 to Abu Dhabi.

On the arrivals board, Etihad flight EY555 from Abu Dhabi was cancelled, as were Emirates flight EK819 and flydubai flight FZ847 from Dubai.

Selected international services are also listed on flight schedules, connecting Riyadh with Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, Italy and the UK.

Scheduled arrivals included Air Cairo flight SM469 from Cairo, Riyadh Air flight RX418 from Manchester and ITA Airways flight AZ838 from Rome Fiumicino.

Outbound services included Riyadh Air flight RX331 to Cairo, flynas flight XY223 to Doha and flyadeal flight F3573 to Istanbul.

The disruption has included flights being sent to alternative airports.

Pakistan International Airlines flight PK725 from Lahore was marked on the arrivals board as being diverted to Dammam, rather than arriving in Riyadh. Pakistan International Airlines flight PK725 from Lahore was marked as diverted to Dammam, while Saudia flight SV885 from Guangzhou was listed as diverted to Jeddah.

Arriving and departing flights remain subject to permission from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation, Reuters reported. Several international airlines have retained suspensions lasting weeks or months.

Travellers should check their flight directly with the operating airline before leaving for the airport and monitor messages about changes to their booking.

Those with onward connections should confirm the status of both flights and ask their airline about arrangements if disruption affects their journey.

Passengers whose services have been cancelled should contact their airline or booking agent to discuss the rebooking or refund options available under their ticket conditions.

Future Forum in Dubai. “Very understandable [that] people will wait and see how the conflict is resolved.”The good thing, Mr Alhawi said, is that even though the conflict been going on since late February, it has helped investors better understand the resilience of the UAE and the capabilities of its government in dealing with a crisis.“I think that's the message that our investors have received over time and I think, maybe not immediately but in the next few years, that will definitely be a positive thing, as more investment is coming,” he said.FDI into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development (Unctad) data.The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July.The UAE has maintained consistent FDI inflow momentum over the targets by 2031.“You'll have some years when it'll grow slightly less or slightly more,” he said. “But now that we've reached the $40 billion [plus] range, we expect to keep that for a couple more years before jumping to the next level, which is the $65 billion range, which is where we want to be.”While various governments at the emirate level are incentivising investors to boost FDI inflows, expanding rail connectivity, and oil and gas pipeline infrastructure.“Now, that investment does two things: one, it shows our confidence in our economy, and two, it shows that we're building different routes and paths for our main value proposition, which is being a logistical hub,” Mr Alhawi said. “We're investing in the right places, which means the investors that are already here can see the impact this will have and they will see it over the next year or so.”Partnerships with investorsThe UAE is more than capable of executing those projects on its own but it is seeking participation of foreign investors in these schemes to make them a part of the UAE growth story.Mr Alhawi said the Ministry of Investment is bringing capital together and is in talks with investors over joint ventures. Options for global investors to team up with the UAE sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices, are also open, he said.“We're super open,” Mr Alhawi said. “I mean, we can build infrastructure ourselves if we want to, but building it with partners makes it makes it more efficient, makes it better, makes it more long term. “We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.”Infrastructure pipelineInvestment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant. HSBC estimates the UAE project finance pipeline is in excess of $190 billion in funding to build the planned the infrastructure projects.The UAE accounts for about 22 per cent of the broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region infrastructure project pipeline of $872 billion, data from HSBC's New Networks of Capital: Menat Infrastructure report indicates. “Ultimately, these large-scale projects, such as Al Maktoum [International] Airport, the Dubai sewage system and developments in Fujairah, have strong government backing,” Mohamed Al Marzooqi, chief executive of HSBC UAE, told The National.“So, these are the paymasters and I don't think we have even touched the surface, to be honest, when it comes to tapping into those financing solutions.” The easiest solution, he said, would be to tap the loan market and financial institutions in the country. They are all “hungry for quality assets 100 per cent here in the UAE”.HSBC, Mr Al Marzooqi said, is not only willing to leverage its own balance sheet, it can also help structure deals in many other ways for project owners and investors. Even with a “complex global and regional operating environment”, international businesses and institutional investors expect the region to remain and infrastructure investment destination and flows of capital will continue over the rest of the decade, the lender said.The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data has identified the $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion planned and unawarded infrastructure pipeline.The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion,” data shows “Infrastructure planning activity has continued this year, with the pipeline increasing a further 15 per cent to $1.4tn between January and October 2026,” the HSBC report said.

“We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.”

Investment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant.

HSBC estimates the UAE project finance pipeline is in excess of $190 billion in funding to build the planned the infrastructure projects.

The UAE accounts for about 22 per cent of the broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region infrastructure project pipeline of $872 billion, data from HSBC's New Networks of Capital: Menat Infrastructure report indicates.

“Ultimately, these large-scale projects, such as Al Maktoum [International] Airport, the Dubai sewage system and developments in Fujairah, have strong government backing,” Mohamed Al Marzooqi, chief executive of HSBC UAE, told The National.

“So, these are the paymasters and I don't think we have even touched the surface, to be honest, when it comes to tapping into those financing solutions.”

The easiest solution, he said, would be to tap the loan market and financial institutions in the country. They are all “hungry for quality assets 100 per cent here in the UAE”.

HSBC, Mr Al Marzooqi said, is not only willing to leverage its own balance sheet, it can also help structure deals in many other ways for project owners and investors.

The sheer size of the MENAT pipeline underpins the scale of the region’s medium and long-term investment potential despite geopolitical headwinds, HSBC said in the report released on Tuesday.

Even with a “complex global and regional operating environment”, international businesses and institutional investors expect the region to remain and infrastructure investment destination and flows of capital will continue over the rest of the decade, the lender said.

The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data has identified the $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion planned and unawarded infrastructure pipeline.

The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion,” data shows

“Infrastructure planning activity has continued this year, with the pipeline increasing a further 15 per cent to $1.4tn between January and October 2026,” the HSBC report said.

singles.headline: Escalation of tensions around Cuba could destabilize Latin America — Russian MFA
singles.summary: The ministry noted that the republic is going through tough times due to the unprecedented trade, economic, financial and energy blockade
singles.body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Further escalation of tensions surrounding Cuba could destabilize the entire Latin American region, the Russian Foreign Ministry said in a statement commenting on the US issuance of a state arrest warrant for Cuba’s historical leader Army General Raul Castro.

"We would like to emphasize that further escalation of the situation around the Island of Freedom, which is already going through tough times due to the unprecedented trade, economic, financial and energy blockade, could lead to instability across all of Latin America and the Caribbean. If a social explosion erupts in Cuba, people could begin migrating en masse to neighboring countries, risking a social crisis there," the statement reads.
